title: Moving From Side Hustle to Business
summary: Check you are ready → Choose a structure → Register and protect → Plan for growth taxes
subtitle: Make the jump from side income to a business you can stand behind.

blocks.text: A side hustle becomes a business when it earns steadily, serves real customers and starts to need real structure. That moment can feel exciting and a little terrifying, like being handed the keys to a bus. This lesson puts the legal and tax steps in a sensible order, so growing up does not mean growing scared.

To the CRA, you are already a business, even if your income is small. Self-employed income goes on Form T2125 with your personal return, whether you earn $500 or $50,000. What turns a hustle into a business is mostly how seriously you run it.
The staircase in this lesson

“I have to quit my job before I can call myself a business.”
items.text: You can run a real business on the side, with a business number, proper records and registered accounts. Many people do that for years.

blocks.text: Take each step in order, and the jump feels like a staircase instead of a cliff.
blocks.detail: A clear order of small legal and money decisions lets you grow with confidence, and keeps your savings and your sleep safe.
blocks.extra: Section 02 checks whether you are ready to grow.

sections.title: Check You Are Ready to Grow

blocks.text: Growing doesn’t mean quitting your day job tomorrow. Many owners spend a year or two building steady income on the side while they put the right structure in place. Look for three signs first.

items.title: REPEAT DEMAND
items.text: Customers keep coming back or sending friends, without you chasing them.

items.title: A WAITING LIST
items.text: You keep turning down jobs you would love to take.

items.title: LOST SLEEP
items.text: The work is eating into your evenings and weekends, and something has to give.

blocks.text: Before you cut your hours
Your safety net, rebuilt
blocks.detail: What a paycheque used to cover

items.title: Cash cushion
items.text: 3 to 6 months — of household costs, because self-employed income comes in waves.

items.title: Health and dental
items.text: Your cost now — workplace benefits end with the job, so price a personal plan.

items.title: EI special benefits
items.text: 12-month wait — self-employed people can opt in for sickness and parental benefits, then wait a year to claim.

items.title: EI earnings test
items.text: $9,254 — net self-employment earnings in 2025 needed to claim in 2026. The amount changes each year.

blocks.text: Build the cash cushion before you cut your hours, not after. If your household runs on $3,200 a month, three months is $9,600. The calculator shows how many paydays that takes.
Build your cushion before you jump

blocks.text: No one takes tax off your business income anymore. Move a share of every payment into a separate tax account from the first month.
The Voltage Tester
paragraphs: Mehdi Karimi worked as an electrician in Surrey. In the evenings he installed electric-vehicle chargers for neighbours. His goal was to cut his day job to four days a week, so he could spend the fifth day on his own customers. A yellow voltage tester hung from his belt.

By spring he had eleven repeat clients. Then a property manager asked if he had liability insurance, a contractor licence and a business number. The company needed all three before it could give him a bigger contract. Mehdi had none of them.

That night he searched online and found a forum full of advice. A dozen people said the same thing: “Incorporate right now.” Mehdi felt a rush of panic. His finger hovered over a button that offered to set up a company for a flat fee.

He stopped and made a different choice. He would not rush into a company because strangers told him to. He booked an hour with an accountant and brought his numbers. His profit was about $22,000 a year. For now, they agreed, a sole proprietorship with good insurance made more sense. They set a review date and wrote down the profit level that would make him think again.

Mehdi registered his business name and got his business number. He applied to Technical Safety BC for his contractor licence and started pulling a permit for every install. He bought liability insurance and opened a business bank account. Then he sent the property manager his papers.

The manager hired him, and the questions helped. She liked how well he had answered them. By autumn Mehdi had moved to a four-day job. By the next review his profit had passed the level he wrote down, and he went back to the accountant with a smile. The yellow voltage tester still hangs from his belt.

items.title: WHAT MEHDI DID FIRST
list: One hour with an accountant, numbers in hand
Stayed a sole proprietor, with a written review trigger
Name, business number, licence, permits, insurance, bank account

blocks.text: Slow is smooth, and smooth is fast.
blocks.detail: A planned structure, the right paperwork and an honest review date protect your income and make you look as professional as you are.
blocks.extra: Section 04 compares the two structures Mehdi weighed.

blocks.text: The structure you pick decides who is responsible for the business’s debts, how its income is taxed and how much paperwork you handle. The two most common choices for a beginner are a sole proprietorship and a corporation.

items.title: Sole proprietorship
list: Legal identity: You and the business are the same person
Responsibility for debts: Business debts and claims can reach your personal assets
Tax filing: Business income goes on your T1 return with Form T2125
Losses: You report the loss on your own return

items.title: Corporation
list: Legal identity: A separate legal entity
Responsibility for debts: Shareholders are generally not responsible for its debts, though lenders may ask for a personal guarantee
Tax filing: The corporation files its own T2 return within six months of its year-end
Losses: Shareholders cannot claim the corporation’s losses
Setup effort: More paperwork, ongoing filings, and professional fees

blocks.text: Neither structure wins every time. A corporation can offer protection and tax planning choices, but it also brings extra costs and rules. Talk to an accountant and a lawyer about your own numbers before you decide. This lesson explains the choices. It does not pick one for you.
How a small corporation is taxed
Inside a corporation

items.title: Federal small business rate
items.text: 9% — on the first $500,000 of active business income, plus a provincial rate from 0% in Manitoba to 3.2% in Ontario.

items.title: Its own return
items.text: T2 — due within six months of the corporation’s year-end.

items.title: Paying yourself
items.text: Salary or dividends — you pay personal tax when money comes out of the company.

items.title: Extra cost
items.text: Every year — separate books, an annual return and usually an accountant’s fee. Federal incorporation costs $200 online, and each annual return $12.

blocks.text: Lower tax inside a corporation mostly helps when you can leave profit in the company. If you need every dollar to live on, the savings can be small. That is why the choice needs your real numbers.

items.title: “Incorporating means I never have to worry about debts or lawsuits.”
items.text: A lender may ask you to personally guarantee a loan. Directors can also be personally liable if the company fails to send in certain amounts it owes, such as payroll deductions. Insurance and good contracts still matter.

blocks.text: Do these in order. Each one makes the next easier, and together they make you look as professional as you already are.
Five steps to a real business

items.title: REGISTER
items.text: Most businesses register with their province or territory, though a sole proprietor using their own name may not need to. Quebec uses the Registraire des entreprises.

items.title: BUSINESS NUMBER
items.text: A nine-digit CRA ID. In British Columbia, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Saskatchewan you get it when you register with the province. Elsewhere, apply to the CRA.

items.title: LICENCES AND PERMITS
items.text: Check what your city, province and industry require. The free BizPaL tool lists them for your location.

items.title: BUSINESS BANK ACCOUNT
items.text: Separate money makes your records cleaner, your return simpler and your case stronger if the CRA, a lender or a landlord asks.

items.title: INSURANCE
items.text: Ask a broker about liability coverage for your type of work. Contracts and insurance still matter, even inside a corporation.

blocks.text: Regulated trades need more than a business number. Electricians, plumbers, gas fitters and some other trades need a licence and often a permit for each job before they work for the public. In B.C., for example, Technical Safety BC requires a licence to be hired for electrical work and a permit for every EV charger install.
Notes by province, and for your taxes

items.title: Registration
items.text: Rules differ by province. Newfoundland and Labrador has no provincial registration for sole proprietorships, while most other provinces require it in many cases.

items.title: Quebec
items.text: Quebec uses the Quebec Pension Plan and has its own business registry, the Registraire des entreprises, so check its rules.

items.title: GST/HST
items.text: You must register once your taxable sales pass $30,000 over four calendar quarters, or in a single quarter.

sections.title: Plan for the Taxes That Come With Growth

blocks.text: Growth is good news that arrives with paperwork. Watch these lines as your profit rises.
As your profit grows

items.title: Instalments
items.text: $3,000 — net tax owing ($1,800 in Quebec) in 2026 and in 2025 or 2024 means quarterly payments.

items.title: CPP
items.text: 11.9% — both halves, on net earnings from $3,500 up to $74,600 in 2026. Quebec residents pay QPP.

items.title: CPP2
items.text: 8% — on earnings from $74,600 up to $85,000, once profit climbs that high.

items.title: GST/HST
items.text: $30,000 — register once taxable sales pass this in one quarter or over four quarters.

items.title: Review trigger
items.text: Your number — a profit or client count that tells you to revisit your structure.

blocks.text: Your instalments also cover the CPP you owe on your own earnings. Set aside for both from every payment, so the quarterly reminder is a transfer, not a panic.
Your tax calendar as a sole proprietor

items.title: March 15, June 15, September 15, December 15
items.text: Instalment due dates, once the CRA asks you to pay quarterly.

items.title: April 30
items.text: Any balance owing for last year is due, even though your return can wait.

items.title: June 15
items.text: Your return is due when you or your spouse or partner have self-employment income. Interest on any balance still runs from April 30.

blocks.text: Write your review trigger down today. It gives you a calm, planned reason to look at your structure again, instead of a stressful one. Then book a meeting with an accountant before you reach it.

sections.title: Quick Check: Which Step Comes Next?

items.title: Who is responsible for a sole proprietorship’s debts? A. The business alone · B. You personally · C. The CRA
items.text: A sole proprietorship has no separate legal identity, so business debts can reach your personal assets.

items.title: Which form reports a sole proprietor’s business income? A. Form T2125 · B. Form T137 · C. Form T2
items.text: Form T2125 is attached to your personal T1 return. A T2 return is the corporation’s.

items.title: Why set a review date for your business structure? A. So you can change structure when your numbers change · B. Because the CRA requires it · C. So you never have to think about it again
items.text: Your best structure can change as your profit and risk change.

items.title: Where do you report self-employed income as a sole proprietor?
items.detail: On your T1 return, using Form T2125.

items.title: In a corporation, can shareholders claim the corporation’s losses?
items.text: The corporation’s losses stay with the corporation.

items.title: When must you pay income tax by instalments?
items.detail: When your net tax owing is above the CRA’s threshold in the current year and in one of the two years before.

items.title: You owe a $2,000 balance for last year and file on June 15. When was the money due?
items.text: Self-employed people can file later, but interest on a balance starts after April 30.

items.title: In one sentence, describe the first step you will take toward becoming a business.
items.text: I will open a business bank account and book an hour with an accountant next month.

blocks.text: Grow in order: check readiness, choose a structure with advice, register, protect the business, plan for tax, and set a review date.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Next Three Steps

blocks.text: Answer for where you are today, not where you hope to be. “Not yet” is a useful answer, because it tells you what to do next.

items.title: Corporation
items.text: A business that is a legal person, separate from its owners.

items.title: Sole proprietorship
items.text: A business owned by one person that is not incorporated.

items.title: Program account
items.text: A CRA account for one tax, such as GST/HST.

items.title: Business number
items.text: A nine-digit number the CRA uses to identify your business.

items.title: Shareholder
items.text: An owner of a corporation who holds shares in it.

items.title: Instalments
items.text: Tax payments you make during the year instead of all at once when you file.
